lesson.title: Selection, Insertion, or Merge: Which Sort Wins?
lesson.summary: Selection sort, insertion sort, and merge sort all produce the same correct output, but they differ sharply in time complexity, best-case behavior, and memory use, which is what actually determines which one to reach for.
lesson.body:
You now have three working sorting algorithms, and it is worth stepping back and comparing them directly using time complexity, since "correct" is not the only thing that matters when a list gets large.

Selection sort is O(n squared) in every case. Its inner loop always scans the entire remaining unsorted portion to find the minimum, no matter what order the elements started in, so a sorted list, a reversed list, and a shuffled list all take the same number of comparisons.

Insertion sort is also O(n squared) in the worst case, such as a reverse-sorted list where every new element has to shift past everything already placed. But it is adaptive: its best case, an already-sorted list, is O(n), since the inner while loop barely runs at all.

Merge sort is O(n log n) in every case: best, worst, and average. It always splits the list in half and merges the halves back together the same way, regardless of the input's original order, so its performance does not depend on how sorted the input already was.

These growth rates look similar on paper but diverge sharply as n grows. For a list of 1,000 elements, n squared is 1,000,000, while n log base 2 n is roughly 1,000 times about 10 (since 2 to the 10th power is 1,024), or about 10,000: selection sort and worst-case insertion sort do around 100 times more work than merge sort on the same input. Scale up to 1,000,000 elements and the gap becomes extreme: n squared is a trillion, while n log base 2 n is roughly 1,000,000 times about 20, or about 20,000,000, a difference of about 50,000 times fewer operations for merge sort.

Time is not the only cost, though. Selection sort and insertion sort both sort the list in place, rearranging elements within the original list using only a small, constant amount of extra memory. Merge sort, by contrast, needs extra memory proportional to the list's size, O(n), to hold the temporary left and right slices created at every level of recursion before they are merged back together. So merge sort trades memory for speed.

All three algorithms, despite their very different strategies, are required to produce the exact same final order, since correctness does not depend on which algorithm you pick:

import random

data = list(range(1000))
random.shuffle(data)

selection_result = selection_sort(data.copy())
insertion_result = insertion_sort(data.copy())
merge_result = merge_sort(data.copy())

print(selection_result == insertion_result == merge_result == sorted(data))

That comparison prints True, because selection sort, insertion sort, and merge sort are all correct sorting algorithms, just with different time and space tradeoffs. In practice, insertion sort's simplicity and adaptiveness make it a good choice for small or nearly-sorted lists, while merge sort's O(n log n) guarantee makes it the better choice as lists grow large. Python's own built-in sort() and sorted() use an algorithm called Timsort, which was designed by Tim Peters specifically to combine ideas from both: it uses insertion sort on small runs of data and a merge-based strategy to combine larger runs, taking advantage of the strengths of each.
